assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a clean new regime of light-matter interaction, with single microwave photons strongly coupled to a superconducting artificial atom on a chip. It is the conceptual and practical basis for dispersive readout, qubit coupling, bosonic encoding and much of microwave quantum optics. The idea is original, the experiments make a basic quantum phenomenon visible and controllable, and the impact is lasting across devices and laboratories.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf (with the Yale experimental and theory collaboration) form a coherent theory plus experiment configuration for the 2004 proposal and first strong-coupling demonstration. The supplied credit does not include Andreas Wallraff, who led the first experiment, so the three-person split among the listed names is imperfect and the experimental credit is not fully represented. I choose the three listed names as the most defensible configuration.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of independent confirmation in many groups, with the architecture now standard in every major superconducting processor. Interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes this a natural follow-on, though the committee should avoid recognising the same platform too quickly.
uncertainties: Wallraff is absent from the supplied credited names, so the experimental attribution is incomplete.
Possible perception of overlap with the 2025 prize, and my own proximity to the superconducting circuits community may call for care about conflicts of interest.
Whether the committee prefers the foundational light-matter physics over the quantum-computing application.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect introduced a new classification of band insulators, protected by time-reversal symmetry, and launched a very large field. The theory was followed by an experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells, with a clear signature of helical edge transport. It is original, conceptually clean and of lasting importance.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposals. Molenkamp led the HgTe experiment (with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposing the HgTe route, and Moore, Balents, Roy and Fu-Kane on the three-dimensional generalisation). The listed three form a natural theory plus experiment trio, but the credit for the HgTe prediction and the 3D extension is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with extensive independent confirmation, including 3D materials by ARPES. Practical applications are limited, but the discovery stands on its own. Recognition is timely or somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and the 3D generalisation is not represented in the supplied names.
Interplay with the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions may make some members regard this as incremental.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength idea and its refinement to the 10^-18 level, redefined the limits of time measurement and has made new fundamental-physics tests possible, such as the search for variations in constants, tests of relativity at millimetre scales and a possible redefinition of the second. The physics is clear, and the experiments pay attention to every physical detail.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept, and Ye's group drove it to record accuracy. Hall and Hansch were recognised in 2005 for comb technology and Wineland in 2012 for ion clocks, so the credited pair is a defensible fit. Contributions from several other groups (for example Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley's teams) are not represented.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories have built optical lattice clocks reaching comparable stability, and the redefinition of the second is under discussion. This is mature and robust, and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize on ion-based quantum measurement and the 2005 comb prize.
Contributions of other groups (e.g., Lemonde, Ludlow and others) are outside the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in these systems launched twistronics and moire quantum matter. The theory-experiment pairing is clean, and the field is large and productive, with tunable correlated and topological phases.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key theoretical prediction. Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators made the decisive experimental discovery, with Cao as first author. The credited trio is a natural theory plus experiment configuration, but Cao and others (e.g., Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov, Kim) have significant claims for the correlated-state work.
assessment.maturity: The central findings have been reproduced by multiple groups, but the interpretation of the superconductivity and the strongly correlated phases is still debated. The prize might be a bit early, although the field is very active and robust.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity is not settled.
Sample inhomogeneity and reproducibility of device-level details.
Credit for the experiment extends beyond the listed names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of single neutral atoms with Rydberg-mediated entanglement made a new quantum simulation and computing platform. It has produced controlled many-body states, quantum phases and error-corrected logical qubit demonstrations. The originality is in combining optical tweezer arrays with Rydberg blockade, and the impact is rising rapidly.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Lukin made key proposals on Rydberg gates and blockade, and Browaeys's work on tweezer arrays and Rydberg interactions is central. Other significant contributors (Jaksch, Zoller, Weiss, Regal, Ahn, Birkl, Greiner, Endres and Bernien) are not in the supplied names, so the credit allocation is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by several groups, with fast progress. The platform's ultimate scientific yield, especially in fault-tolerant computation, is still ahead of us, which makes the recognition somewhat early.
uncertainties: Broad group of contributors and unclear credit.
Whether the discovery is a physical regime or an engineering platform.
Possible prematurity relative to error-correction results.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Mott insulator transition and a range of Hubbard-type systems, giving direct access to strongly correlated many-body physics with single-site resolution. It is an important, lasting experimental programme that changed how many-body physics is studied.
assessment.attribution: The theory (Jaksch, Zoller, Cirac) and the experiments (Greiner, Bloch, Esslinger) are both central. The five-name list cannot all be included, and the choice of experimentalists leaves out the founding theory. A prize may need to split between theory and experiment in a way that is difficult to settle.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and independently reproduced in many laboratories, although quantum simulators have not yet answered open questions such as the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram at low temperature.
uncertainties: Theory versus experiment credit allocation.
Overlap with the 2001 prize on Bose-Einstein condensation and the 2012 prize.
Limited uniquely new regime relative to the promise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation are conceptually essential: they show that arbitrarily long quantum computations are possible in principle with noisy hardware. The surface and toric codes underpin the practical roadmap of superconducting platforms. The ideas are original and deeply influential.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane constructed the first codes, and Kitaev proposed topological codes and anyonic fault tolerance. Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov, Ben-Or and Preskill have strong claims, so a three-person prize is hard to justify fairly.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of below-threshold error suppression are very recent, so the physical vindication is only just arriving. As a theorist embedded in experiments I find this important, but the Nobel is for discovery, and the practical promise is still ahead of us. It may be premature as a physics prize.
uncertainties: Fairness of credit among many contributors.
Whether this is physics or computer science and mathematics from the committee's viewpoint.
Experimental vindication is early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for interferometry began with Caves's proposal and was demonstrated experimentally by Slusher, Kimble and others, then engineered into gravitational-wave detectors. It uses a basic quantum-optics effect to beat the standard quantum limit in a real instrument, which links foundational quantum optics to a major scientific facility.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal, Kimble's group made the early squeezing demonstrations, and Schnabel and others advanced the practical squeezed-light sources for GEO600 and LIGO. Slusher, Walls and Xiao, Wu, Kimble, Mavalvala and McKenzie and others also have important claims, so allocation is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is used in operating LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, so it has been confirmed in a demanding setting. However, the credit complexity and the fact that the major observational prize was already given for gravitational waves makes the timing uncertain.
uncertainties: Contested credit among many contributors.
Whether the discovery is separate enough from the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
